title: Nor do they deny the power to act otherwise: neither the act nor grace removes it
source_text: XXVII. Et similiter quum dicunt falsum esse quod agens liberum, positis omnibus quae sunt ad agendum requisita, possit agere, & non agere, hoc & illud agere, sententia eorum non est, per ea quae ad agendum praeparant & impellunt, ab agente libero tolli facultatem aliter agendi, aut actionem suspendendi: quandoquidem agnoscunt facultatem illam per actum ipsum non tolli; nedum per ea quae ad agendum impellunt. Nec enim negant eum qui per Dei gratiam egentis miseretur, in se semper habere potestatem non miserendi, & qui mundi hujus voluptates contemnit, retinere facultatem illas quaerendi atque amplectendi, quae per divinam gratiam ab eo non aufertur. Adeoque non aliud intendunt quam hoc, positis omnibus quae requiruntur ad agendum, contingere non posse ut agens liberum non agat: licet alioqui maneat in eo facultas qua posset non agere, aut aliter agere. Exempli gratia, fieri non posse quin positis omnibus quae ex parte Dei necessaria sunt ad fidem & conversionem hominis producendam, homo convertatur & credat; quanquam semper, & etiam quum credit & convertitur, in eo maneat facultas, qua non credere & non converti posset.
pass_a_gloss: And likewise when they say it is false that a free agent, all things being posited which are requisite to acting, can act, and not act, do this and that, their opinion is not, that through those things which prepare and impel to acting, the faculty of acting otherwise, or of suspending the action, is taken from the free agent: since they acknowledge that that faculty is not taken away through the act itself; much less through those things which impel to acting. For they do not deny that he who through the grace of God pities the needy, has always in himself the power of not pitying, and that he who despises the pleasures of this world, retains the faculty of seeking and embracing them, which is not taken from him by divine grace. And so they intend nothing else than this, that all things being posited which are required to acting, it cannot happen that a free agent not act: although otherwise there remains in him the faculty by which he could not act, or act otherwise. For example, that it cannot be but that, all things being posited which on God's part are necessary to producing the faith and conversion of a man, the man be converted and believe; although always, and even when he believes and is converted, there remains in him the faculty, by which he could not believe and not be converted.
pass_b_english: In the same way, when they say it is false that a free agent, given everything required for acting, can act and not act, and do this and that, they do not mean that whatever prepares and drives him to act takes away his ability to act otherwise or to hold the act back. They acknowledge that the act itself does not remove that ability, much less the things that drive him to it.

They do not deny that someone who by God's grace shows mercy to the needy always keeps in himself the power not to show it, or that someone who scorns this world's pleasures keeps the ability to pursue and embrace them; God's grace does not take that ability from him.

Their only point is that once everything required for acting is in place, a free agent cannot fail to act, even though he otherwise keeps an ability by which he could refrain or act differently. For instance, once everything needed on God's side to produce a man's faith and conversion is in place, the man cannot fail to be converted and believe, though always, even while he believes and is converted, he keeps an ability by which he could fail to believe and be converted.

choices.why: Kept as the Schools' technical term; Le Blanc fixes its sense as a real power to act otherwise, not a state of balance between options.
